title: Kylian Mbappé: Real Madrid star seeks to defuse anger in China after Mao ‘dictator’ comment | CNN
text:
Source: Reuters

FrancesoccercaptainKylian Mbappéapologized to China on Tuesday after a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator, underscoring how swiftly global celebrities can come unstuck.

In a video on a ​French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappé is heard discussing a funny meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator.”

“During a recent interview, I ‌reacted to an image of myself,” Real Madrid forward Mbappé said in a statement. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.

“I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” added Mbappé, who has ties with firms includingSwiss sportswear brand OnHolding, hotel chain Accor, and Lego. “This was absolutely not my intention.”

The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative China market, where satire about Mao, modern China’s founding leader who ruled the country ​from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.

LaLiga President Javier Tebas said that he held a meeting with the ambassador of China in Spain to address the situation and “seek solutions that ​allow us to overcome this episode.”

“Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of ⁠Chinese fans who follow our competitions,” Tebas said in a statement posted to social media. “China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for LaLiga.”

Other major organizations that have incurred the wrath of Beijing and ​Chinese netizens include fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana, Swiss watchmaker Swatch and the National Basketball Association.

Some recovered quickly while others took years.

Brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage ​said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappé effective immediately.

The companies said they “firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.”

China’s state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving LaLiga and Mbappé, and all advertisements involving Mbappé have been removed, state-backed media outlet the Paper reported on Tuesday.

“Mbappé’s team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about,” said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. ​Burns Sports Group.

Swiss-based On Holding, which signed Mbappé in September after he had spent two decades at US rival Nike, welcomed his apology and said it had “deep respect” for China.

Accor did not immediately respond to requests for ​comment.

Denmark’s Lego, which has a Mbappé building set on sale in China, said it could not comment. The Mbappé set still featured on Lego’s Chinese website on Tuesday.

Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappé’s remark had “triggered ‌a backlash ⁠among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence.”

“What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,” the state-backed Global Times added. “The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn’t get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance.”

On Chinese social media platform Weibo, one user wrote about the apology; “Not accepted. Not forgiven!!”

State broadcaster CCTV struck a more conciliatory tone, however, saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say after his apology, and “even more importantly” watch what he does.

“We hope La Liga, Real Madrid, and Mbappé himself will genuinely learn a lesson from this, offer a ​sincere apology, and thoroughly correct their mistakes,” CCTV said in ​a statement.

Real Madrid declined to comment.

Tebas issued ⁠an apology earlier on Tuesday on X and said his organization deeply regretted the alleged comments that have caused discomfort and offence in China.

“We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation,” Tebas wrote. “A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a ​single episode.”

As of 7 a.m. GMT, four topics related to Mbappé were still among the top 10 trending searches on Weibo. Some netizens called for China ​to blacklist Mbappé and reduce his ⁠commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.

Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappé’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for.

Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press.

“In attempting to laugh at himself and his reputation of being a dictator in the locker room, he apparently crossed a red line he didn’t know was there,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at ⁠Annex Wealth Management.

In ​an interview with L’Equipe last month, Mbappé said that although aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting ​him as a dictator showed “a lack of political and human awareness.”

A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people “will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society.”
